idiom_name: struct version snapshots (value semantics) + Array.last(where:) over effective dates
implementation_notes: Swift's value semantics do the heavy lifting: a Version is a struct, so assigning or passing it copies and a published snapshot cannot be edited through another reference. The continuity is a struct (or a class kept private) holding versions ordered by effective Date, and as-of is last(where:) over that array - the array is the temporal collection and the stdlib supplies the search; firstIndex(where:) gives the insertion point for retroactive amendments. Because Date is an absolute instant, effective dates are built through Calendar/DateComponents so that 'effective 1 March' means the same day in every time zone; stdlib collection copies are copy-on-write, so publishing costs nothing until an amendment is inserted.
pitfalls: Date is an instant, not a calendar date: comparisons ignore how the value was built, so 'effective on 1 March' must be constructed with Calendar in an explicit time zone or it silently means local midnight elsewhere.
Value semantics are shallow for reference members: a Version holding a class instance shares that instance with every copy - keep snapshot types to value types (arrays and dictionaries are fine).
Date carries no time zone; only Calendar/TimeZone give it meaning, and DateFormatter is expensive - build dates from components rather than parsed strings on hot paths.
Amending through a let-bound continuity requires var/mutating; if the continuity is made a class for sharing, access from multiple threads needs @MainActor or a lock around the history.
